analysis.one_liner: Makes the 2001 income tax rate cuts permanent instead of expiring in 2010.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never received a House vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2001 Bush tax law (EGTRRA) cut income tax rates across all brackets but included a "sunset" — the cuts were written to end after 2010 so the long-run budget cost would look smaller. This bill would strike that sunset for the income tax rate cuts, making them permanent. Because the rate structure is proportional across income but the dollars are not, the largest tax savings in dollars go to the highest earners: the top rate fell from 39.6% to 35%, while lower brackets saw much smaller percentage cuts. The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Households with the highest taxable incomes gain the most, since they pay the largest share of income tax and benefit most from keeping the lower rate schedule permanently. The top rate alone dropped four and a half percentage points under the 2001 law, a cut that applies only to income above the highest thresholds. All filers in the lower brackets also keep their reduced rates, but in dollar terms their savings are far smaller.

how_it_helps.text: The bill removes the 2010 sunset on the income tax rate cuts in Title I of the 2001 tax law, so the reduced rates would no longer expire by law.
Making the cuts permanent means high earners do not face the scheduled return of the 39.6% top rate, locking in the lower rate structure indefinitely rather than through 2010.

analysis.who_pays: The Treasury — and ultimately taxpayers through borrowing or future taxes — bears the cost. Permanence converts a temporary, budget-rule-limited tax cut into a standing revenue loss, and the distribution of the loss is tilted toward the top of the income scale, which is where the dollars concentrate.
analysis.who_pays_short: The federal Treasury and future taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Removing the sunset turns a temporary tax cut into a permanent revenue loss for the federal government, adding to deficits and debt unless offset by spending cuts or other taxes.

The savings concentrate at the top: the top rate was cut from 39.6% to 35%, so the largest dollar benefit of permanence goes to the highest-income filers, while a standing revenue loss must eventually be paid for by someone.

The sunset was a structural feature of the 2001 law designed to fit the cut within Senate budget rules; repealing it without addressing the underlying cost sidesteps the constraint the drafters built in.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a real, continuing benefit to households across the income scale in the form of lower rates, but the dollars are heavily weighted toward high earners, and the full revenue cost lands on the federal budget permanently. An honest assessment is that this is a permanence bill for the top of the income distribution wrapped in the language of a rate cut for everyone.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it never came to a floor vote before the 108th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Patrick Toomey introduced the bill on February 13, 2003, to strike the sunset on the 2001 law's individual income tax rate cuts.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
No further action was taken: the committee never reported the bill and the House never voted on it during the 108th Congress.
Only two representatives cosponsored the bill, both Republicans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No constituency gained. The rate cuts stayed temporary on paper, so the scheduled post-2010 return to the higher rate schedule remained the law, and the federal government's future revenue was left unchanged. High earners simply did not get the permanence they would have received.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one gained; the cuts stayed temporary

for.name: Rep. Patrick J. Toomey
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make the 2001 income tax rate cuts permanent.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never took it up, so it never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the only record of support is three Republicans (the sponsor and two cosponsors), and no Democrat was on record either way.

industries.note: Permanence of the rate schedule delivers its largest dollar savings to the top brackets, including the full value of the top-rate cut from 39.6% to 35%. The cost is a standing federal revenue loss that someone else eventually pays for, so the interest runs against ordinary taxpayers' stake in a balanced budget.
Converting the temporary rate cuts to permanent law removes the 2010 expiration and creates an ongoing revenue loss, which ordinary taxpayers ultimately bear through debt service or future taxes.
